title: Patricians and Plebeians
objective: After this level you can explain the Conflict of the Orders between Rome’s old families and ordinary citizens.
summary: Plebeians won rights from the patricians over two centuries, starting with a walkout in 494 BCE and ending with the Hortensian law of 287.

cards.headline: What if the workers and soldiers of a city simply walked out?
cards.body: In Rome, they did. It was the opening move in a fight over who got a say, and it lasted about two centuries.

cards.headline: Two kinds of citizen
cards.body: Every Roman citizen was one of two kinds. Patricians belonged to Rome’s old aristocratic families. Plebeians were all the rest. In the early Republic, patricians held the priesthoods and, by tradition, the magistracies too, though some historians think a few plebeians also held early offices. Either way, the top jobs belonged mostly to one side. Rome had thrown out its king, but not its old families.

cards.headline: The walkout
cards.body: In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians tried something bold: they walked out of Rome in protest. They refused to work or fight until they won concessions. A city nobody will work or fight for is just a pile of buildings. Their long struggle for political rights, about two centuries of it, is called the Conflict of the Orders.

cards.headline: Plebeians win ground, one step at a time

events.label: Plebeians walk out: the first secession
One of the two consuls may now be a plebeian
The Hortensian law makes plebeian assembly votes bind all Romans, ending the Conflict

cards.headline: The orders: reconciled
learned: Walkouts won them rights over two centuries
The Hortensian law of 287 BCE ended the conflict

questions.prompt: What did the plebeians do in 494 BCE to win concessions?

options.label: Elected a king of their own
Moved the whole city to a new site
options.rationale: They left, but only in protest.

options.label: Walked out and refused to work or fight

questions.explanation: In the first secession, plebeians left Rome and withheld their labor and military service.

questions.prompt: Why was a plebeian walkout such a powerful tactic?

options.label: Rome depended on plebeians to work and fight
Plebeians owned all of Rome’s land
options.rationale: The patricians held much of it.

options.label: The gods punished anyone who stayed

questions.explanation: Without plebeian farmers, workers and soldiers, Rome couldn’t function or defend itself.

questions.prompt: From Level 13: before the Conflict of the Orders, who filled the magistracies, and so the Senate?

options.label: Plebeians elected by lot
options.rationale: Plebeians were shut out at first.

questions.explanation: Patricians held the magistracies, and the Senate was made up of former magistrates.
